subject: 0binomial model crashes on HPC but runs correctly at personal computer at home

messages.author: 9dc4da17f4e4d0d4
messages.subject: 0binomial model crashes on HPC but runs correctly at personal computer at home
parts:
Dear INLA Community,
I’m reaching out to seek guidance regarding an issue in case it may be resolved by adjusting model options.
I'm currently trying to fit a 0binomial model in INLA for a small country dataset, which includes approximately 900 unique locations. Despite several attempts over the past week, I’ve been unable to get the model to run successfully on the university’s Ubuntu-based HPC servers. Interestingly, when I ran the same scripts on my personal machine at home, the model converged within 60 seconds without any errors or warnings.
Unfortunately, I can’t rely on my home setup for this analysis, as the broader goal is to scale the model for predictions across the entire continent—starting with tests on individual countries.
I’ve attached the full verbose output below. The HPC currently supports R versions 4.4.2, 4.4.1, and 4.3.2.
I would appreciate any advice or suggestions—especially if there are additional settings or options that might help ensure the model runs smoothly on the HPC.
I am getting the following error when trying to fit the model:
GitId: "devel"
Error:12 Reason: The Newton-Raphson optimizer did not converge
Message: Condition `lambda < 1.0 / lambda_lim' is not TRUE
Line:1013 Function: GMRFLib_init_GMRF_approximation_store__intern

Segmentation fault


You ask for 16 x 1 = 16 number of threads,
which is more that I got from the system: 8
Number of threads is reduced to 8:1

 *** WARNING *** GMRFLib_2order_approx: rescue NAN/INF values in logl for idx=242


You ask for 16 x 1 = 16 number of threads,
which is more that I got from the system: 8
Number of threads is reduced to 8:1



GitId: "devel"
Error:12 Reason: The Newton-Raphson optimizer did not converge
Message: Condition `lambda < 1.0 / lambda_lim' is not TRUE
Line:1013 Function: GMRFLib_init_GMRF_approximation_store__intern

Segmentation fault
Error in inla.inlaprogram.has.crashed() :
  The inla-program exited with an error. Unless you interupted it yourself, please rerun with verbose=TRUE and check the output carefully.
  If this does not help, please contact the developers at <he...@r-inla.org>.
Calls: inla ... do.call -> inla -> inla.core -> inla.inlaprogram.has.crashed
In addition: Warning message:
In inla.core(formula = formula, family = family, contrasts = contrasts,  :
  The A-matrix in the predictor (see ?control.predictor) is specified
  but an intercept is in the formula. This will likely result
  in the intercept being applied multiple times in the model, and is likely
  not what you want. See ?inla.stack for more information.
  You can remove the intercept adding ``-1'' to the formula.
Execution halted
Below I am attahcing the output file with verbose turned on.
Thank you in advance for your help.
Best regards,
Christos

messages.author: 9a89594e7fcb7aad
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] 0binomial model crashes on HPC but runs correctly at personal computer at home
parts:
Please install the most recent testing version

INLA_25.06.22-1

which you can download from

https://inla.r-inla-download.org/R/testing/src/contrib/

and install via

R CMD INSTALL INLA_....

if you're using R-4.4 (should go fine, unless you're using 'rgeneric'). 

with R-4.5 you can do inla.upgrade(testing=T)

for HPC, I usually just compile R myself and install it locally, as the versions
are 'always' way behind, and INLA is compiled for 4.5 only now.

for '0binomial', you might want to add

control.inla=list(cmin=0)

which avoids wrong signed hessians, which can appear for these zero-inflated
models. I guess this will solve your issue. If you're concerned about the effect
of 'cmin', then you might do

r <- inla(..., control.inla=list(cmin=0))
r$.args$control.inla$cmin <- -Inf
r <- inla.rerun(r)



Best
Havard

        control.inla=list(cmin=0)

r <- inla(..., control.inla=list(cmin=0))
r$.args$control.inla$cmin <- -Inf
r <- inla.rerun(r)



Best
Havard
